title: An energy budget as stacked areas: where does the energy go?
summary: Kinetic, potential and dissipated energy are stacked in time, so their sum is the total. A dashed line at the starting energy shows where the total should sit. For a damped oscillator, mechanical energy drains steadily into heat.

media.alt: A stacked area chart over 12 seconds: green kinetic humps at the bottom, a blue potential layer above them, and a large amber dissipated layer growing to fill the plot up to a dashed white line at 10 joules, with text 'sum = 10.0 J' at three times.
media.caption: Reference render of class F4.5 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: Where does the energy go?
read_the_figure.axes: x: time in seconds, 0 to 12. y: energy in joules, 0 to 12.2. Layers from the bottom: kinetic (teal), potential (blue), dissipated (amber). Dashed white line: the conserved total, 10 J. The legend is below the plot.
look_at: At t = 0, how is the energy split? How does it change by t = 1?
What happens to the kinetic and potential layers together as time passes?
Does the sum always equal 10 J? How was the amber layer obtained?
How big is the mechanical part (kinetic + potential) at t = 12?
as_drawn: The system is a damped oscillator with gamma = 0.18 per second and frequency 2.2 rad/s, starting at rest with 10 J of potential energy.

The three 'sum = 10.0 J' labels are true by construction: the amber layer is computed as 10 - kinetic - potential, so the total cannot fail to be 10. It is not an independent check that energy is conserved.

The mechanical energy falls to about 1.4 percent by 12 s (exact oscillator: 0.0138 of the start; e^(-2 gamma t) gives 0.0133), so the amber band takes over almost all the plot. The legend sits on top of the x-axis label.
read_the_figure.proves: That a model with friction loses mechanical energy at the rate shown and that the plotted shares add up to the starting value. The total is an input here; it does not prove the model conserves total energy.
if_wrong: Dissipated energy defined as the remainder: any error in KE or PE is hidden in the heat layer.
Stacked layers with no baseline for the middle layer: its size cannot be read.
Energy in different units or time steps for the layers.

terms.meaning: Energy of motion, one half m v squared.
Stored energy, for a spring one half k x squared.
Mechanical energy converted to heat by friction or damping; it is lost to the mechanical system.
The total, including heat, stays constant for a closed system.
The rate gamma at which the oscillation amplitude decays, e^(-gamma t).

remember: Total energy = kinetic + potential + dissipated: constant for a closed system.
dE/dt = -2 gamma v^2: mechanical energy only decreases.
Mechanical energy decays at twice the amplitude rate: e^(-2 gamma t).
Show the total and compute dissipated energy independently if you want a test.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Areas stacked in time: the thickness of each layer at a given time is that part of the energy, and the top of the stack is the total. Teal, blue and amber name the three forms. The dashed line marks the starting energy and acts as the reference for the stack.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Energy conservation is a bookkeeping statement: parts change, the total does not. A stack makes the bookkeeping visible, so the eye sees the energy slosh between kinetic and potential and drain into heat. Because the mechanical energy decays smoothly while the layers oscillate, the plot shows both the fast exchange and the slow loss.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Only the bottom layer sits on a common baseline: the thickness of the middle layer must be read as a difference. Defining heat as the remainder makes the sum equal to the total by construction, so a leak in the model (or in a numerical integrator) would be hidden. Stacked areas hide small layers. And the legend position can cover an axis label, as here.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: A drawn conserved total gives the eye a line that the stack must touch. Printed totals at several times let a reader see that it does. These are the checklist items, but they test the model only if the dissipated layer was computed separately, by integrating the dissipation, not as the remainder.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Plot kinetic, potential and the mechanical total as lines on a log axis to see the exponential decay. Compute heat independently as the integral of 2 gamma v squared and plot the residual, which should be zero. A Sankey diagram shows flows. For several cycles, plot the energy per cycle as bars.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Compute Q(t) by integrating 2 gamma v^2 and draw the residual 10 - K - U - Q as a thin panel below; add a log-scale line of K + U against t to show the decay rate.

steps.title: Mechanical energy only decreases
steps.tex: \begin{aligned}\ddot x+2\gamma\dot x+\omega_0^{2}x&=0,\qquad E=\tfrac12\dot x^{2}+\tfrac12\omega_0^{2}x^{2}\\[4pt]\dot E&=\dot x\bigl(\ddot x+\omega_0^{2}x\bigr)=-2\gamma\dot x^{2}\le0\end{aligned}
steps.note: A numerical solution with gamma = 0.18 and omega = 2.2 confirms dE/dt = -2 gamma v^2 to 7e-5. The energy falls fastest when the speed is largest and is flat at the turning points, which makes the staircase steps in the blue and amber layers.

steps.title: Decay of the envelope
steps.note: Energy decays at twice the rate of the amplitude, because it is quadratic in the amplitude. After 12 s only about 1.3 percent is left, which is what the plot shows.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) what is the energy split at t = 0? (2) How long until the mechanical energy halves? (3) How much is left at t = 12 and how do you know the amber layer's 9.85 J is not independent evidence?

solution.text: All potential: the blue layer reaches the 10 J line, kinetic is zero (the body is released from rest).
About 1.9 s: the envelope of K + U drops from 10 J to 5 J at roughly the second hump.
About 0.14 J of mechanical energy (1.4 percent). The amber layer is 10 minus that by construction, so it shows the sum is 10 only because it was defined so.

worked.answer: All potential at the start; mechanical energy halves every 1.9 s; 0.13 J left at 12 s; the amber layer is a remainder, not a check.

analyze.q: Why is the dissipated layer a poor check of energy conservation as drawn?
The kinetic layer touches zero at regular intervals. Why, and how often?
How would an integrator that adds artificial energy show up in this plot, and how in a plot with independent heat?

evaluate.q: A simulation reports 'energy conserved to 1e-12' because the plotted sum is flat. What would convince you?
evaluate.hint: Independent dissipation integral and its residual.

create: Compute the dissipated energy by integrating 2 gamma v^2 and plot the residual.
Draw the same budget for an undamped oscillator and for a heavily damped one.

checks.q: What does the dashed line at 10 J represent, and why must the stack touch it?
checks.answer: The conserved total of the closed system: kinetic + potential + dissipated must equal the starting energy.

checks.q: Energy amplitude decays as e^(-0.18 t). How fast does the energy decay?
checks.answer: As e^(-0.36 t): twice the rate.

checks.q: A budget plot shows total = 10 J at all times. Does that prove the code conserves energy?
checks.answer: No if heat is computed as 10 minus the rest; the sum is then 10 by construction. Compute heat independently and plot the residual.
